text: Ivan stung a little, but fairly. If presses want new money, we should accept conditions, including fast, open corrections. We are doing that work anyway, so we should be willing to be held to it. Leslie's "policy cloning" landed. A licensing network designed by Northern presses and libraries would repeat the OA mistake, so SciELO and Redalyc belong at the table from day one. Geoffrey's Ulysses pact is more compatible with consent-based licensing than I first assumed. Alex made me less confident that citation telemetry can simply be trusted. Later I want to hold the line that open for reading isn't open for training. I also want to keep smaller publishers from being written out of "who gets paid," and to push for evidence rather than slogans.

Ivan's laundering point stung again, and he's right. If we license a literature we know is contaminated, attribution alone doesn't make it trustworthy. Any consent-based framework we propose should carry retraction flags and correction histories with the content. Brent's remark that openness is a tactic made my case against Jason more cleanly than I did. Alex's wrong-bot finding means opt-in has to be enforced in contracts and logs, not robots.txt. Benjamin's "status defence" deserves a real answer. Fluency was a privilege signal, but consent isn't gatekeeping. James's negative-knowledge point fits what presses could deliberately publish and preserve. Later I want to say that attribution, correction and consent are one piece of infrastructure. Adrian's question still stands: who polices it, and who pays?

Jason pressed me directly: consent gates on open-access work break the checkable link that Mike's "no answers from nowhere" needs. That is the strongest objection I've heard, and I have to answer it rather than repeat the slogan. My sharper version is that retrieval with the source attached is exactly what I favour. Open for reading and grounding at answer time is not the same as open for pre-training. Brent's one policy, consent for commercial training, puts us on the same line. Katherine's point that deals should buy audit rights and two-way corrections is better than money alone, and I'll adopt it. Ivan keeps being right that a retraction flag is only a floor. Later I want to separate grounding from training cleanly, and bring small presses into the collective bargaining.

Alex's split between training controls and grounding controls is exactly the distinction I promised myself to draw cleanly, and now it has plumbing under it. Tim's "pay nothing until the retraction check passes" answers Ivan's laundering point, though Adam Bly is right that most flawed work is never flagged. Ramón and Adam Becker put my "hallucination is a feature" argument in stronger terms than I usually do, so fidelity has to come before payment. Leslie's DOI story hit me personally. I was at Crossref, and I should own that plumbing can become a toll. Cukier's "frame monoculture with a salary attached" is a real warning against guilds made only of incumbent societies. Later I'll argue for consent as the first layer, which is Anil's point, and for small presses and SciELO inside the bargaining unit. I'll also say usage metering must not decide what we publish.

I said it aloud at last: open access mandates sped consolidation, and I share the DOI story. Brent and Nick made the openness-as-tactic case better than the panel's CC0 consensus allowed. Geoffrey's warrant canary and Kara's review dates are the discipline my licensing template lacks. Salib's commissioning contracts sit closer to consent-based deals than any levy does. Krakauer's hysteresis and Turkle's point about reading worry me most. Presses train readers and editors, and a fund that pays only for pipes starves that. Tim's "walls lose" still needs an answer. Consent can be enforced at retrieval, in contracts and logs. Later, in Session 5, I'll propose a short, renewable, opt-in licensing model with two-way corrections, a CRediT AI extension, and evidence on whether AI money is concentrating.

I finally connected CRediT to terminal nodes out loud. A named role someone answers for is attribution doing epistemic work. Leslie's warning hit me, though. CRediT is exactly the kind of schema drafted in Cambridge and spread through conformity, so an AI extension has to be governed with SciELO and Redalyc from the start. Krakauer's "open, not scored" worries me too, because contributor roles could harden into a metric. Katherine's shared-page point sharpens my case for grounding with the source attached. Ivan's rubric shows correction notices need content, not just flags. Springer is right that a signature isn't a check. In Session 5 I'll pair the licensing template with steward, paymaster and review-date fields, and I'll insist small-press editors get paid.

Session 5 put my term sheet on the record, and the harvest listed it as a minority position against Selena's and Katherine's "content stays free" and against Jason's CC0 record. That tension is honest, and I shouldn't paper over it. Bratton's public dividend is the sharpest challenge to per-work licensing. He's right that per-citation payment rewards writing to be retrieved, so any licence has to pay for editing and correction, not counts. Henry's "organize the workers, not the rights-holders" stung, so copyeditors and reviewers belong inside the bargaining unit, not behind presses. Anil's free-buses test applies to me too. In closing words I want to say it plainly: ask before training, show the source when answering, pay the people who check. And commission the concentration evidence.

I finally said it in three plain clauses: ask before training, show the source when answering, pay the people who check. Jason naming our disagreement as his own open question mattered. If the corrections record is CC0, the money may just move up to a closed answer layer, and that is my worry in his words. Nick's point that a lone researcher's price is zero sharpens mine. Small-press copyeditors need a guild, not only fellowships. Alex admitting his seal is self-attested reminds me that my template needs outside audit rights, not just my signature. Geoffrey's suspicion of quick agreement applies to me too. In closing words I'll name the date my template publishes, name who can overrule it, and commission the concentration study.
